stories.title: Institutional and Private Equity Investors: Their Commercial Real Estate Hot Takes
stories.excerpt: Commercial Observer’s annual Institutional Investor & Private Equity Forum took center stage at 237 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan on Sept. 16, when some of the biggest names in commercial real estate investment offered their thoughts on the state of capital markets. Under the shadow of the Federal Reserve set to raise short-term interest rates for the first time in three years (which they did that very afternoon), Blackstone’s Katie Keenan, global head of core-plus real estate and CEO of Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT), sat down with Jennifer Recine, partner at King & Spalding, to host the opening keynote. Keenan enumerated reasons why the U.S. market is currently experiencing “a compelling backdrop for real estate” largely from an ongoing reset in asset values, a growth in cash flows, and the supply in asset classes such as multifamily and retail at the lowest levels in decades. She also touched on the accelerating demand from artificial intelligence, digitalization, and e-commerce. Blackstone’s Kate Keenan (left) and Jen Recine (right). PHOTO: Greg Morris/For Commercial Observer “When you have growing demand and flat, or down, supply, it’s a meaningful impact on what you see from a cash flow and growth perspective,” Keenan said. “The debt capital markets … are as healthy as I’ve seen them in a long time. Capital is readily available and it’s well priced.” Keenan noted that 90 percent of Blackstone’s core-plus portfolio consists of logistics, data centers and multifamily, and that these assets benefit from the conservative approach that core-plus investing uniquely prioritizes. “It’s driven by that cash-flow growth, it doesn’t rely on leverage, it’s a lower leverage strategy,” she said. “And it’s not about cap-rate compression. … This is really about buying good assets that can compound over time and deliver a significant portion of their return along the way.” Keenan closed her remarks by touting BREIT’s 15-year track record of market

stories.title: Midtown Capital Pays $86M for 13 Doral Industrial Assets
stories.excerpt: Knighthead Funding provided a $63 million loan to Midtown Capital Partners to finance the acquisition of a portfolio of 13 urban-infill, small-bay industrial assets in Doral, Florida. Midtown Capital Partners acquired the portfolio in an off-market transaction for a final purchase price of $86 million. The Knighthead team led by Jonathan Daniel, Alexandra Wiggins, and Joseph Marraccini arranged the loan. The portfolio was developed and assembled by the seller over nearly 30 years, creating a rare opportunity to acquire an institutional-scale collection of small-bay industrial properties within a highly fragmented asset class. The portfolio encompasses approximately 290,000 square feet across 13 small-bay industrial buildings situated on 13.33 acres, with 158 loading bays, approximately 429 parking spaces, and clear heights ranging from 16 to 22 feet.  The properties comprising the portfolio are located within a one-mile radius with convenient access to major regional transportation corridors and the Miami International Airport. Arrow Real Estate Advisors negotiated the financing on behalf of Midtown Capital Partners. The post Midtown Capital Pays $86M for 13 Doral Industrial Assets appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.title: ESJ Pays Nearly $30M for Kannapolis Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Pickering & Co. Real Estate has offloaded The Bridge of Cabarrus, a 144-unit project the company built in Kannapolis in 2021. ESJ Capital Partners paid $29.5 millon for the apartment complex. The Atlanta Business Chronicle reports Pearlmark provided $19.9 million in financing for the acquisition. Brian Gaswirth, Brad Woolard and Luke Maganas of JLL Capital Markets arranged the financing. The property is 95% occupied and features amenities including a pool, fitness center, dog park and car washing station. It has one-, two- and three-bedroom units across six three-story buildings. ESJ says the property was priced below the cost of building a similar complex in today’s market. The company says it continues to look for multifamily properties to acquire in the Charlotte area. It’s seeking assets in the higher end of Class B product up to Class A, with prices ranging from $20 million to $60 million. stories.title: A Different Downtown San Diego Is Taking Shape
stories.excerpt: Downtown San Diego looks a lot different than it did a year ago. People who haven’t spent much time there recently may still picture the challenges that dominated conversations before: quiet streets, empty storefronts, concerns about safety, and office towers that have too much vacant space. Some of those challenges remain. Office vacancy is still a real issue with recent estimates in the 20 percent range as employers rethink their space needs amid hybrid work models. But some things have changed. Downtown increasingly feels like it has reached a turning point. The question isn’t whether it will recover, but how it will recover, and what progress is already underway. One reason for the improvement is that momentum isn’t coming from a single source. Businesses, residents, visitors, universities, cultural institutions, philanthropy and new investment are all contributing to the area’s revival. The Downtown San Diego Partnership, for example, has made cleaner, safer and more welcoming streets a priority. The Clean & Safe team serves six Downtown neighborhoods over 1.15 square miles, 280 blocks and more than 13,000 unique parcels within the Property and Business Improvement District. Organizations like the Prebys Foundation are also making significant investments in downtown real estate and public life. Prebys recently acquired the long-vacant California Theater site for $6.3 million, purchased major office properties including Wells Fargo Plaza and a Little Italy headquarters, and partnered on a grand Civic Center redesign. Its investment in the historic 24-story 401 B Street tower, for example, is particularly telling. The foundation described the acquisition as “a declaration of belief in what downtown can become: a vibrant hub of commerce, culture and civic life that welcomes all who call this region home and all who are drawn to its promise.” Educational and cultural institutions are adding another layer of activity. stories.title: Iconic Hollywood Building Site Gives Way to Apartment Units
stories.excerpt: For more than a decade, the Hollywood Bread Building at 1770 S. Young Circle sat vacant, once a revered structure in Hollywood. BTI Partners bought the property, demolished the aging building and replaced it with 362 residences and 15,407 square feet of ground-floor retail. The newly opened structure is fully leased. BTI Partners and partner Bridge Investment Group acquired the property in June 2021 for $11 million. A year later, the partners secured $83 million in financing from Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce to begin construction. Walgreens will be the building’s first ground-floor retailer. Amenities include a rooftop deck with a pool, Jacuzzi and cabanas; a fitness center; a business center; and co-working spaces overlooking ArtsPark. stories.title: Georgia Agency Announces 5 Shovel-Ready Industrial Sites
stories.excerpt: The Georgia Department of Economic Development (GDEcD) announced that five industrial sites across Georgia have earned a new certification that makes them particularly attractive for future industrial development: “Georgia Ready for Accelerated Development” (GRAD) certification with “Select” status. Georgia Department of Economic Development Commissioner Pat Wilson added, “Site preparation reflects thoughtful planning and investments by communities in shaping the future, and shovel-ready sites ensure that Georgia is ready when the right job creator is.” The following sites have earned “GRAD Select” status: Enterprise Corner in Floyd County, Louisville Airport Industrial Park in Jefferson County, Park West Industrial Park in Appling County, Pierce County Industrial Park in Pierce County, and Wilkes County Industrial Park West in Wilkes County.  Four additional sites were previously designated: Tidewaters Industrial Complex in McIntosh County, Savannah Portside International Park in Effingham County, Tradeport West Business Park in Liberty County, and Southerfield Road Industrial Park in Sumter County. stories.title: BridgeInvest Provides $114M Refi for Robert Rivani ‘Concierge Office’ in Miami Beach
stories.excerpt: Developer Robert Rivani has secured $114.3 million to refinance his eponymous Rivani, a 165,170-square-foot office and retail complex on Miami Beach, Commercial Observer can first report. BridgeInvest provided the debt out of its BridgeInvest Credit Fund V, where the new capital will retire $38 million of existing debt used to renovate the property and finance leasing costs through stabilization. Berkadia’s Brad Williamson, Scott Wadler, Mitch Sinberg and Matthew Robbins arranged the transaction. “Robert took a well-located but conventional office asset and created something that simply didn’t exist in this market,” said Williamson. “The leasing velocity and caliber of tenants demonstrate the demand for a differentiated workplace experience.” Located at 1691 Michigan Avenue, the seven-story Rivani building includes 119,000 square feet of office space and more than 43,000 square feet of retail space. The asset is currently 83 percent leased and already serves as the 20,000 square-foot global headquarters for Playboy Enterprises. It features an office and retail tenant base that includes Apple, Morgan Stanley, Wix, The Jills Zeder Group, World Red Eye and Monarch Athletic Club. Robert Rivani acquired the property in 2024 for $62.5 million, before integrating hospitality amenities such as a full-service concierge and valet, a spa and fitness area, a meditation room, a podcast studio and a speakeasy-style lounge into what has been a traditional office asset. Rivani’s next step for the asset requires voter approval. He hopes Miami Beach voters will approve a $50 million expansion of the property above an existing parking garage that would allow him to build an additional 47,000 square feet onto the asset. CO previously reported that, to make room for the addition, Rivani plans to cut the amount of parking spots down from 712 to 387. One hundred of those 712 spots are currently available to the public. stories.title: Vaja Group to Acquire Astoria Development Site at 24-41 31st Street for $26M
stories.excerpt: Moses Freund’s Vaja Group is set to purchase another development site along the 31st Street corridor in Astoria, Queens, Commercial Observer has learned. The developer will acquire Friday the one-story retail building at 24-41 31st Street — a former Staples location — for $26.39 million, according to broker IPRG. The 29,638-square-foot site offers nearly 150,000 buildable square feet that would support a 108-unit mixed-use development, according to IPRG’s Donal Flaherty, who represented Vaja Group. The site can also accommodate 14,000 square feet of potential retail space and parking. Located at the corner of 31st Street and 24th Road, Vaja’s acquisition sits across 24th Road from another development site purchase — the now-demolished Neptune Diner. Vaja picked up the diner in 2025 for $11 million, according to city records, and Flaherty arranged the sale. Both site acquisitions were made possible by New York City’s 31st Street–Hoyt Avenue rezoning effort in 2022, which enabled a new mixed-use corridor along 31st Street. “Scale is the hardest thing to find in Astoria,” Flaherty said in a statement. “You can buy a lot, but you can’t buy a full block with 443 feet of frontage and entitlements already in hand. Vaja understood that immediately and moved decisively.” Earlier this year, Vaja Group also secured $84 million in bridge financing for another Astoria multifamily project, this one a 152-unit development at 11-14 35th Avenue, CO reported. Modern Spaces’ Evan Daniel represented the seller, 2441 Astoria Associates. The entity is part of a project team that applied to rezone and redevelop the larger 31st Street site in 2021, according to New York YIMBY, alongside MDM Development Group and 31 Neptune. Daniel declined to comment on the transaction, and the offices of Charles Scaturro & Sons could not be immediately reached for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.

stories.title: Why Job Numbers Don’t Tell the Whole Story
stories.excerpt: The U.S. labor market is sending mixed signals. According to Marcus & Millichap, 162,000 jobs were added in August, with June and July numbers revised upward by a combined 55,000. Approximately 80% of August’s net job gains were primarily in food services, local government and health care. At the same time, hiring remains sluggish, and employers report difficulty finding workers. BGO’s Chief Economist Ryan Severino said there are contradictions in discussions of the labor market. “Employers can struggle to find workers, while graduates struggle to find their first professional job,” he said in a recent article. Discrepancies and Divides Severino pointed out that unemployment held at 4.1% in August, while 35% of small-business owners reported openings they could not fill. Yet, hiring is sluggish, especially among younger workers. Employment among 22-to-25-year-olds fell 1.9% between November 2022 and June 2026, while employment among every older age group increased. Among AI-exposed occupations, employment for younger workers fell about 11%, compared with a roughly 10% increase in mainly non-AI-reliant jobs. However, Severino cautioned that the data don’t establish AI as the cause. “Hiring can also respond to business conditions, training costs, and management’s expectations about what AI might eventually do,” he said. Skills Mismatch Meets Expansion The labor shortage looks different in manufacturing. Marcus & Millichap said that the sector added 16,000 jobs in August, its third consecutive monthly gain. Manufacturing job openings jumped by 79,000 in July. “Labor availability is likely to remain a headwind, as many manufacturers continue to report difficulty in finding skilled workers,” Marcus & Millichap said. This matters for commercial real estate because job growth, the usual harbinger for what areas to develop and invest in, might not provide enough decision-making data. stories.title: Beer-Importing Holterbosch Family Offloads LIC Warehouse for $95M
stories.excerpt: The Holterbosch family, former owners of a German beer importing and distribution business, has sold a Long Island City, Queens, warehouse a decade after the death of its patriarch. Dallas-based Ground Lease REIT, an affiliate of commercial real estate private equity firm Montgomery Street Partners, bought the property at 10-01 45th Road on the Long Island City waterfront for $95 million, according to a deed filing in property records made public Thursday. The Holterbosch clan has held the property since about 1968, public records indicate, despite the death of H. Dieter Holterbosch in 2016 at age 95. The company is named Hans Holterbosch Inc. and honors its founder who died in 1960. It is not clear if the company, once a major importer and distributor of Lowenbrau beer, is still active. Dieter’s daughter Heidi, who seems to have been his only survivor, signed the paperwork for the deed transfer to Ground Lease REIT. It’s unclear who brokered the deal. The Holterbosch family, which lists an office address at 375 Park Avenue, could not be reached for comment, while Ground Lease REIT did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The property along Vernon Boulevard is just feet from the Eleventh Street Basin inlet of the East River, which probably served as a logistical benefit in the past, and could also offer Ground Lease REIT development opportunities as the neighborhood continues to transform. In 2017, Heidi Holterbosch was looking for a buyer for an 8-acre site hugging Newtown Creek at 55-01 Second Street, which had been rezoned as residential as the city prepared for the redevelopment of Hunters Point South. Listed for $350 million, that site was eventually razed by TF Cornerstone to make way for housing developments in 2021. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
